planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Arctic Snow was hybridized by Patrick Stamile and registered in 1985.

directions: Arctic Snow bears large ivory flowers with a soft green throat on scapes standing roughly two feet tall, part of Patrick Stamile's run of pale and near-white tetraploid introductions from the mid-1980s. Blooms open midseason with extended daily flower life, giving each bud a longer-than-average display before closing. The dormant foliage forms a tidy, vigorous clump that benefits from division every three to four years to maintain bud count. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the cleanest flower color.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Anastasia, registered in 1984, is credited by hybridizer-history sources as Jeff Salter's first daylily introduction.

directions: Anastasia holds a place in daylily history as the first cultivar registered by Jeff Salter, who went on to become one of the most prolific American hybridizers of the following decades. The clump forms a vigorous, floriferous stand of strap-like foliage topped by well-branched scapes in summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigor and bloom count. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for best performance.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Stout Lime Frost was registered by Patrick Stamile in 1990.

directions: Stout Lime Frost shows a pronounced greenish throat and a notably glittery diamond-dusted petal surface, a trait Patrick Stamile favored in several of his late-1980s and early-1990s introductions. Well-branched scapes carry the flowers above vigorous, dormant foliage for a midseason display. Established clumps increase steadily and are best divided every three to four years to keep flowering strong. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; White Crinoline was registered by Patrick Stamile in 1992 from Ptarmigan crossed with tetraploid Gentle Shepherd.

directions: White Crinoline carries near-white, green-throated flowers that are noticeably fragrant, an unusual trait Patrick Stamile bred into this early-midseason introduction from his long run of white-toward daylilies. The dormant clump reblooms later in the season under favorable conditions, extending the display well beyond a single flush. Well-branched scapes hold the six-inch flowers above tidy foliage. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and divide every three to four years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Creative Edge was registered by Patrick Stamile in 1993 from a cross of (Plum Candy x Winter Mint Candy) x Admiral's Braid.

directions: Creative Edge shows cream-lavender petals with a purple eye zone, chartreuse throat, and a gold-touched purple edge, a combination growers at the time considered groundbreaking for edged daylily breeding. The fragrant flowers open on well-branched, semi-evergreen scapes through midseason with reliable rebloom. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring to keep the distinctive edge pattern displaying at full size. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Early Snow was registered by Patrick Stamile in 1996 from White Hot crossed with Alpine Snow.

directions: Early Snow produces huge near-white flowers, up to seven inches across, with a glowing yellow-green throat and shimmering, diamond-dusted ruffled petals that open wide and flat. It blooms early in the season and reblooms later on vigorous dormant scapes, rounding out a long display from a single clump. The fragrant flowers make it one of the standout entries in Stamile's decades-long pursuit of a true white daylily. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and divide every three to four years.

common_name: Daylily 'Smoky Mountain Autumn' (Lenington Award Rose Blend Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Smoky Mountain Autumn was registered by Lucille S. Guidry in 1986 and won the AHS Lenington All-American Award in 1997.

directions: Smoky Mountain Autumn carries rose-blend flowers with a darker rose-lavender halo and olive-green throat on a compact, early-blooming scape under two feet tall. Its proven performance across varied climates earned it the Lenington All-American Award, which recognizes daylilies with exceptional garden adaptability. Clumps rebloom under good conditions and build into dense, floriferous stands within a few seasons. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and divide every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Daylily 'Little Fruit Cup' (Extra-Early Strawberry Eyezone Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Little Fruit Cup was registered by Lucille S. Guidry in 1988.

directions: Little Fruit Cup bears cream flowers marked with a vivid strawberry-red eyezone above a green throat, opening on modest scapes among Lucille Guidry's run of extra-early-blooming introductions. Its small stature and bright contrast make it well suited to the front of a border or a mixed perennial bed. The clump bulks up readily and benefits from division every three to four years to keep bloom counts high. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the most vivid eyezone color.

common_name: Daylily 'Butterpat Twist' (Extra-Early Cream Pink Blend Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Butterpat Twist was registered by Lucille S. Guidry in 1989.

directions: Butterpat Twist produces soft cream-pink blend flowers with a green throat, opening extra early in the season on scapes under two feet tall. It is one of a cluster of Guidry introductions from the late 1980s bred for dependable early bloom and vigorous clump formation. The strap-like dormant foliage stays tidy through the growing season and increases well by division. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and divide every three to four years to keep the clump productive.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Morning Blossom was registered by Lucille S. Guidry in 1985.

directions: Morning Blossom bears large cream-pink blend flowers with a green throat, held on scapes over two feet tall during an early-to-midseason display. It represents the larger-flowered end of Lucille Guidry's mid-1980s breeding work, pairing generous bloom size with the vigorous garden habit typical of her introductions. Clumps fill in steadily over a few seasons and respond well to division when crowded. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for best flower size and color saturation.
